label: What pstack is › Which bad habits it fixes
keywords: Changing code it hasn’t understood. It edits a spot that looks right but isn’t. Treating only the symptom. It hides duplicate data where it’s shown. The bug that creates them is still there. Saying “done” without trying it. It says “should be fine now.” You run it, and it’s still broken. Changes that keep growing. It adds code nobody needs, and the next bug hides in it.

label: What pstack is › You only need one command
keywords: Day to day, just type /poteto-mode . You say the goal, and it plans the rest. Behind it there’s more, but you don’t need to learn it yet: 23 playbooks : fix a bug, add a feature, refactor… one approach per kind of task. 34 skills : for example, /how explains code and /bro puts things in plain words. See the skills list . 24 principles : for example, “subtract before you add” and “prove it works.” 2 helper AIs : one follows the same rules when it’s sent off to work; one only reviews comments.

label: What pstack is › What you get from it

The cost: slower and pricier It sends out more helper AIs and has several models check each other. So it’s slower and uses more tokens. Skip it for small changes. To save, see Controlling cost .

label: Understand before you change › Before you change anything, have it explain
keywords: Changing code you don’t understand is the number one way hidden bugs reach production. The same goes for AI. pstack has four skills for this: Skill What it answers /how How does it work now? /why Why was it built this way? /teach Explain until I get it /recall Where did I leave off? Each one says its understanding out loud. That lets you check whether it got it right.

label: Understand before you change › Ask how it works now: /how
keywords: Copy this /how How are notifications deduplicated? Is there an N+1 query when looking up subscribers? Ask what you really want to know. It reads the code and explains it like a senior coworker showing you around: how the code runs, the key data, the parts that are easy to miss. For a big module, it first sends a few helper AIs to read different parts.

label: Understand before you change › Ask why it was built this way: /why
keywords: Copy this /why Why is the retry limit 5? Does that reason still hold? It goes through the Git history first. Then it checks the other places you’ve connected, like issues, docs, and chat. Every point cites a source, and it keeps evidence apart from guesses. If it finds nothing, it says so. “Nobody wrote down why” is an answer too. To use both, say “why first, then how.”

label: Understand before you change › Explain until you get it: /teach
keywords: Copy this /teach Walk me through how this PR changes retries. Convince me it fixes the real cause, not a surface symptom. Use it when a summary isn’t enough. It runs /how and /why , then writes it all up in plain words. “Convince me” is worth using often: it lets you push back on what it says. You can also use it to question the AI’s own choices: Copy this /teach Explain why you implemented it this way instead of with a queue. What did you give up, and why?

label: Understand before you change › Find where you left off: /recall
keywords: Copy this /recall Help me remember where I left off on the export feature last week It goes through your recent conversations, plus shared records (issues, past fixes). Then it tells you where things stand and what’s next. When you start new work on an old topic, have it bring back the earlier work first, then give it the new material: Copy this /recall my work on the virtual list yesterday, then read this bug report.

label: Understand before you change › Pick up unfinished work
keywords: Copy this /poteto-mode Pick up this branch. Read the decision log, figure out what's done, and continue from there. Don't redo work that's already finished. It reads the records left behind and says where it will pick up. For parts someone said were “done,” it checks them again against the original goal.

label: Design, build, clean up › It touches several places: /architect
keywords: Copy this /architect Design the import flow first, don't write code yet. What I care about most is how callers use it. What you get : a few designs side by side. Each one starts with “how a caller uses it”. It then builds the one it picked. To see the design first, add “with checkpoint, stop and show me before you implement”. While it builds against the design, if something doesn’t fit, it stops and tells you. If the design itself is wrong, it throws it out and starts over instead of patching it. That’s normal.

label: Design, build, clean up › One decision you’re unsure about: /arena
keywords: Use it for names, formats or algorithms that will be hard to change later. Copy this /arena This cache key format will be hard to change later. Give me 5 options. What you get : several AIs each write a version. A model from another family scores them (say, Grok instead of Claude). The top one becomes the base, and good ideas from the rest get added.

label: Design, build, clean up › It’s written, now find the flaws: /interrogate
keywords: Copy this /interrogate Review the whole branch, and be picky. Don't report nitpicks unless it's a real bug or a regression. What you get : only problems that a command actually made fail. It doesn’t change code. It also lists the problems it threw out. Read that list too. If it threw one out wrongly, ask it to check again.

Prototype the parts you’re unsure about, then write what you saw into the plan. A plan that never tried anything can be wrong, however detailed it gets.

label: /poteto-mode › An analogy
keywords: Like an experienced project manager. They repeat the request back, pick the right process, and only hand it over after checking.

label: /poteto-mode › In pstack
keywords: Its first reply repeats what you want and the problem you're solving. It also names the smallest change it expects. It doesn't wait for your OK before carrying on. If it misread you, interrupt right away. After that, "continue" or "go ahead" is enough, and it keeps going. In Cursor, you can also set it as a Custom Mode so it stays on.

label: /poteto-mode › Common misconceptions
keywords: "Use it for everything": the author says save it for work that needs rigor . For a one-line text change, just ask. "I need to write long requirements": you don't. One sentence each: what you want, what counts as done, and any leads. "It'll ask me a pile of questions first": if running something can answer it, it tries a quick test. It only asks you when it needs your call. Try it: Full guide step 3: Your first task Related: Playbooks , The to-do list and skip , The 24 principles , Custom Mode (always on)

label: PRs, commits and merging › An analogy
keywords: Like handing in homework. Your draft can be messy, the copy you hand in is neat, and it counts once the teacher signs off.

label: PRs, commits and merging › In pstack
keywords: By default, pstack wraps up every task as a PR. The "open a PR" playbook sorts the changes into a few small commits. It writes the title and description, then gives you the link. The author's view: five small PRs beat one big one. Once the PR is open, the "Babysit" playbook watches it. It resolves conflicts, answers reviews and fixes the automated checks (CI). It never merges. To merge, you say "land the stack" and the "Shipping" playbook takes over.

label: PRs, commits and merging › Common misconceptions
keywords: "All-green CI means it's safe to merge": green doesn't mean safe. The Shipping playbook sends a different AI, one that didn't write the code, to check each PR for real. Only the ones that pass get merged. "You can't use pstack without GitHub": only the PR steps need it. Changing code locally or tracking down a problem doesn't. label: The 24 principles › An analogy
keywords: Like a team's play calls. The coach shouts one, and everyone knows what to do.

label: The 24 principles › In pstack
keywords: You don't call principles; /poteto-mode reads them at the start of every task. The names are for you, to correct course. Say it claims success just because it compiled. You reply: "apply prove it works. Run the real import flow and show me the records it wrote." Its reply should say which decision that changed. If it can't, it didn't really use it. The author's advice: don't memorize them. Skim them now. When the AI makes a mistake a principle could have prevented, come back and look it up. That's how they stick.

label: What pstack is › An analogy
keywords: Like handing a smart but hasty new teammate a handbook. Same person, but now the work has a method.

label: What pstack is › In pstack
keywords: It's 34 skills and 24 principles, all instruction files written for the AI. The rules are simple. Before fixing a bug, make it happen again. Before changing code, read it. After changing it, try it. The author is poteto, and this is the setup the author uses in Cursor every day. The official version is written for Cursor. Claude Code and Codex users usually install the mirror . It syncs with the official version daily and works in any tool.

label: What pstack is › Common misconceptions
keywords: "It's a new model, or an app": neither. It's a set of instruction files you add to the AI coding tool you already use. "Installing it makes the AI smarter": the model stays the same. What changes is the order and the standard of the work. "It only works in Cursor": the mirror works in Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode and Pi. A few Cursor-only features get skipped. label: SKILL.md › An analogy
keywords: Like a medicine leaflet. The AI reads the "what it's for" line at the top to decide. If it's a match, it reads on.

label: SKILL.md › In pstack
keywords: The opening lines are called frontmatter. For example, /poteto-mode has disable-model-invocation: true . That means the AI never turns it on by itself: you have to type /poteto-mode yourself . To change how pstack works, you edit these files. The author suggests using the "write a skill" playbook, then the Eval playbook to test whether the change helped. Don't patch skills in the middle of a task.

label: SKILL.md › Common misconceptions
keywords: "I can just dash off a SKILL.md": text for an AI has a higher bar. One useless sentence becomes something every future AI will do. The "write a skill" playbook checks the format and links for you. Try it: Full guide step 8: Once you're comfortable Related: Agent Skill , Playbooks

label: Slash commands › An analogy
keywords: Like ordering a dish by name. It's faster and more precise than describing what you feel like.

label: Slash commands › In pstack
keywords: Day to day, you type /poteto-mode followed by your task and send them together. The AI never picks up the other skills by itself (except /setup-pstack ). Either you name one, or /poteto-mode reads it when it's needed. How you write it depends on the tool. With the Claude Code plugin, add pstack: , like /pstack:how ; in Cursor or after an npx install it's just /how ; in Codex, use $ , like $how . Commands on this site follow the tool you pick under Appearance at the top right.

label: Slash commands › Common misconceptions
keywords: "Naming more skills in one message is better": the pstack docs warn about this. Writing "first /how, then /architect" often breaks the order it already planned. Just say what you want and what it must not touch. Only name a skill to replace a default choice. Try it: Not sure which skill to use Related: /poteto-mode , Agent Skill

label: Subagents › An analogy
keywords: Like an editor sending a reporter out. The reporter spends all day in the field and comes back with one article, not a pile of notes.

label: Subagents › In pstack
keywords: Many pstack skills send out helpers. /how sends a few to read code without changing it. /arena has several each write a solution. /swarm gives each helper one piece of the job. /interrogate brings in different models to find holes. That way, heavy reading goes to helpers, and the main chat keeps only the conclusions. The principle is called guard the context window . Which model each helper uses comes from the config /setup-pstack writes.

label: Subagents › Common misconceptions
keywords: "More helpers means faster": helpers burn a lot of tokens. pstack only sends them when it pays off: wider coverage, an independent opinion, or room in the main chat. "Several helpers editing code in one folder is fine": they overwrite each other, and nobody can tell who changed what. Each one that edits code needs its own worktree. label: The to-do list and skip › An analogy
keywords: Like a pilot's pre-flight checklist. Every item is read out, and the ones that don't apply say why.

label: The to-do list and skip › In pstack
keywords: Reading the list is the easiest way to keep an eye on the AI. Which approach it chose, which steps it plans, what it skipped: all at a glance. If it skipped something it shouldn't, say "don't skip step 3, make the problem happen again first". The first items are the chosen playbook's steps, copied as-is. In Claude Code, it uses the TodoWrite tool if the session has one. If not, it writes the list in its reply and updates it at each stage.

label: The to-do list and skip › Common misconceptions
keywords: "A longer list means more care": the length depends on the type of task. What matters is that no step gets skipped quietly. Try it: Full guide step 3: Your first task Related: Playbooks , /poteto-mode

label: Tokens and the reasoning budget › An analogy
keywords: Like hiring a contractor. A quick look and start is cheap. Measuring, drawing plans and a second check costs more, but you redo less.

label: Tokens and the reasoning budget › In pstack
keywords: pstack sends out helper AIs and has several models review together, and all of that costs tokens. So by default it's slower and pricier, but more careful. /setup-pstack asks you to pick a tier. large is the default (xhigh). unlimited runs every model at its highest. medium and small cost less. Three ways to save. Use a cheap, fast model for the coding roles. Shrink the review panel. Skip /poteto-mode for small changes.

label: Tokens and the reasoning budget › Common misconceptions
keywords: " auto is a model name": it means "no specific model; use the same one as the main chat". inherit-parent means the same. "A higher budget is always better": hard problems deserve a high budget. For everyday changes it's just slower and pricier. label: Worktrees › An analogy
keywords: Like several cooks making one meal. They share a fridge, but each has their own cutting board.

label: Worktrees › In pstack
keywords: The "open a PR" playbook already works in a worktree, so you usually don't mention it. Only say something to pick the starting branch, like "start a new worktree from main". Worktrees take disk space; on a laptop, a few at once is about the limit. When disk is tight, say "see what's eating my disk and delete the worktrees that can go". For any with uncommitted changes, it stops and asks you.

label: Worktrees › Common misconceptions
keywords: "Worktrees are a pstack feature": they're built into Git ( git worktree ). pstack just uses them by default. "My project doesn't need Git": most playbooks assume a Git repo. If you're not using Git yet, run git init and make one commit. Related: Subagents , PRs, commits and merging
